about: What this plugin is known not to hold. A limit written only in prose is lost the next time someone reads past it, so every one of them has a row here and the row is checked. `where` names the records that state it: `dNNNN` a decision record, `spec` the specification, `handoff` the handoff page, `escapes` the escapes ledger, `trials` the trial protocol. `plan` is the disposition the owner locked on 2026-11-13; a row never silently changes plan. Closed rows stay, so that a claim can be checked against what closed it.

areas.guide: The skill that walks a person through the layers of a new design system.
areas.adopt: The skill that records what a repository already has, without changing it.
areas.audit: The read-only report on how far a repository has got.
areas.find: The read-only search of the store, nearest store first, before something new is built.
areas.inventory: The read-only inventory of the store: what each store holds, the state of each piece, six kinds of finding, and what it could not look at.
areas.intake: The command that takes a block into the store for a need, by the ladder of three rungs, every choice the owner's on the decision sheet.
areas.change: The command that retires a block of the store, or merges it into the block of another need, after saying what it reaches, on the owner's answer.
areas.core: The command that reads the first repository of a product family, lays out the lock-or-default sheet, builds the family core from a person's answers, and checks a core's shape.
areas.status: The read-only report on what waits on the owner and what to run next.
areas.decide: The sheet of every question that waits on the owner, and the answers written back.
areas.document: The document a command hands over, set on the frame every document shares.
areas.checks: The gate tool and the browser test it installs.
areas.rules: The page a screen-building agent reads before it starts.
areas.specimen: The sheet that draws the options on the repository's own screen.
areas.book: The handoff book drawn from the repository.
areas.reference-app: The example application this repository carries as its proof.
areas.trials: The runs by independent agents that test the plugin.
areas.upgrade: The command that brings the installed tool into a repository, the stamp it writes, and the version it compares.
areas.capabilities: The table of what a user of a design system needs done, its sockets and plugs, and the checks that hold it.
areas.review: The read-only review of one drawn screen: its pictures, the two things it measures on them, the pack it writes for a reviewer and the record it hands over.
areas.brief: The read-only brief of one screen: the twelve slots of its sheet, what reads each, and the sheet it hands over.

kinds.partial-check: A check holds less than the ledger row it proves claims.
kinds.no-check: A rule is written down and nothing holds it.
kinds.wrong-signal: A report or a check can mislead the person reading it.
kinds.stack-bound: It works only on one kind of repository.
kinds.unproven: It is built, but nothing independent has exercised it.
kinds.conflict: Another document in the system tells a builder the opposite.

plans.fix: Meant to be closed by this project; the roadmap says when.
plans.keep: Accepted as it is, stated here so nobody counts on more.
plans.hand-off: The fix belongs to another repository, named in `repo`.

The files of a retired block stay in the core under blocks/<need>/, so the same need is not promoted again: the promotion refuses it, and core --check names a store that offers a need retired.json keeps. A block for that need is promoted under another need.

Tier 3 reads the member's copy and never the core folder, so a block the core retired is still offered by find and taken by core --take until a person accepts the retiring (core --accept, or core --join pinning again): until then core --moved, status and inventory say it was retired, and the repository wins by its pin.

A proposal carries the value a member holds, or the block's files as it has them, never a hold: a member that wants a lock lowered says so in its reason, and the family's owner lowers it with core --change. A rule is not proposed, its words being its row's.

A proposal for a block is made against the core's block as it was, by the hash that named it: once the core's block changed, granting it is refused, the owner refuses it with that reason, and the member proposes again from the newer block.

Proposals are files of the core folder: the family's owner sees them only where the folder is reached (core --proposals), a proposal made on one machine reaches another only by the core's own repository, and the first line of a session says a proposal waits in every member, not only where the owner works, since the plugin does not know who the owner is.

An answer or a block taken out of the core by hand, or by a plugin older than retired.json, is still read as retired, and once a member accepts it its mark and its row say the core names no one and does not say why: only a retiring made with core --retire carries who, when and why.

The core learns what a repository answered, and which blocks of the core it uses, only when a person runs core --report or pins the core again: taking a block in writes the repository alone and says the report is behind, as core --moved and status do where the core's folder can be looked at. Until then the store's entry does not name the repository under used_by, and a block two repositories use still says no second use; on a machine that cannot reach the core's folder nothing says the report is behind.

The commands find and intake read the needs the family's other repositories answered from the member's copy of the core, as of its pin: a need told to the core after the pin is not said until the member pins again, and the copy holds neither what the core retired nor what its owner refused or granted, so a need retired or refused since is still said, with the step that asks. The move that asks (core --propose --graduate) reads the core's folder and refuses with who retired or refused it, when and why; core --moved says when a report in the core is not the one copied.

Two repositories are seen to have answered one need only when both keep it under the same need key: the periodic line of status counts by key, and a need two repositories keyed otherwise is never counted. find and intake match the words asked against the key, the name and the description a repository told the core, never meaning, as for every store (find-matches-words-not-meaning); and find says a need of the family only where no nearer store answers, so a component of the repository's own that holds the words asked stops the walk at tier 1 and the family's need is not said there: intake, which asks the stores beyond the repository's own, says it (seen on the copy of the second product's package in the trial of decision 0121).

A report tells a block by its need, its name and what it is for, never the adapters it needs, so a block not yet promoted is taken to need what every block of code needs, the components and source adapters: a repository that lacks one of those is not proposed to, and one that lacks another adapter the block needs learns so only once the block is promoted, when tier 3 does not offer it and says why. See also core-promote-adapters-are-a-persons-word.

A row of the intake ledger that does not say what its block is for (description) is left out of the report, and so is a block the core retired that the repository keeps as its own, a piece of the starter kit, and a need that is no key: the report move names each with why, but the family is then not told of that block, and it is never proposed for graduation.

The shape of a core stays 2 and a graduation is a third kind of proposal: plugin 0.67.0, the one version that knows proposals and not this kind, reads a core folder that holds a graduation as not holding its shape and refuses to join or change it until the plugin is updated; older versions do not read proposals at all, and no version reads them from a member's copy.

The first repository of a family, which joins only when its owner says so, reports with core --report --core DIR and is promoted from, but has no look at the core: core --moved, status and the first line of a session read a declaration it does not have, so what the family's owner chose, or that a block of it is asked to graduate, reaches it only through the owner; and find and intake there say nothing of the family's needs.

A graduation granted without the folder of the repository that has the block (--from) promotes nothing: the promotion is owed until the owner runs the call the grant printed, and only core --proposals, the periodic line of status in a member and core --moved of the member that asked say so; the first line of a session counts proposals that wait on an answer and not this one. With --from, the block is written into the store before the proposal records the answer, the two being separate files.

The key used_by of a block records each repository that told the core it uses the block, and no command takes a name out: a repository that left the family, or retired the row of the block, stays named, and second_use never goes back to false. A block the owner refused to graduate is the same block again by its repository and its name only: renamed, it may be proposed again.

A member of a family is named by the main folder of its repository, also when the folder that joined is a package inside it: two packages of one workspace that each declare the family share one line of the core's members and, since slice 2 of item 7.2, one report, the later written over the earlier, and a block either uses is told as used by the repository. Two repositories whose main folders have one name share them likewise.

The promotion refuses a block whose row of the intake ledger names a source the repository does not pin, unless the ledger declares that word as its word for made by hand (values: by-hand), and no command of the plugin writes that line: a repository whose intake ledger names its hand-made blocks by a word of its own has every one of them refused until a person writes the line by hand, and a block taken from an outside source is refused until that source is pinned with its licence line (seen in the first trial of the done-when line of stage 7, where the line was written by hand on the owner's word).

The promotion knows the first repository of a family, as it knows a member, by the name of its main folder as the core's declaration wrote it: a clone or a copy of that repository kept in a folder of another name is refused as neither the first repository nor a member, though it holds the same ledgers (seen in the first trial of the done-when line of stage 7).

The preview of joining (core --join --dry-run) ends as a wrong call when no name is given with --by, so a person cannot be shown what joining would write before saying who joins, though the first step of joining in the skill is that preview (seen in the first trial of the done-when line of stage 7).

The preview of intake (--dry-run), as text and as data, names the file of the waiting list it would write and not the words of the question in it, so a person cannot read what they will be asked before the file is written (seen in the first trial of the done-when line of stage 7).

On a repository of a family, the decision sheet counts each row the core answered as answered, and lists it under «refused or given another answer, and no command changes anything for it yet», since its note is not the word keep: the rows a member only inherits read there as refusals nothing acts on (seen in the first trial of the done-when line of stage 7).

The preview of adopt puts the family question first and holds back what a core this machine knows answers, and still prints, in the same preview, the questions no core answers: that the person is asked the family question alone, before those, is said by the skill and held by nothing, as is the guide asking it before any layer. With several cores known, a question any of them answers is held back, so a repository that joins a core that does not answer it is asked that question one preview later.

Adopt puts the question about a locked answer held otherwise on the decision sheet only for a value the repository's ledgers hold, which for the source colour is the token file: where a run lays no token file (no gate can run the tool, or the token check could not be made to fail), no question is written and the line says so. A default the repository holds otherwise is recorded, in the run that first writes its row, as the repository's own answer from before it joined, under the name of the person who joined: nothing checks that the value is older than the joining.

On a member whose ledger has no row for the source colour because it holds a colour its core locks otherwise, the audit's next line, and the then line status copies from it, still say the colour is to be confirmed with a person; that line leads to adopt, whose line names the core's question about the difference, and status and the decision sheet no longer list the colour as a call of the person.

An icon set that is a package is pinned by the version package-lock.json pins it at, and that file alone is read: a repository whose packages another package manager locks gets no row from icon-source or adopt, and the pin of a row a person wrote is not compared there, which the reader says.

The gate holds the pin of an icon set row, not its use: a screen that imports icons from another icon package, or writes an svg element of its own, is not red. Slice 2 of item 12.1 (spec 0017, criterion 8) adds the list of known icon packages and that check.

The check icon-set-use reads an import as written (from, import and import() with a plain name): a package reached through require, an import() whose name is built while the code runs, or a module of the repository's own that only passes on another package's icons, is not seen.

The icon set the guide recommends to a repository with none is said by icon-source when the guide or a person runs it with no package or folder: status and audit do not list it, so a repository with no icon set row reads as before (spec 0017, criterion 1).

The wall names the mark by the id of its row, logo:<id>, as spec 0017 writes the item: once the owner kept logo:<id>, a later branch that changes a file of that row again passes the wall on the same answer, and only the check of the pins and the licence hold the new files.

The check logo-use reads the app frame as the adapter of the build gives it: on one build the files right under src/, on the other the layout files of the app router and the modules of the repository they import, one step down. On a build whose adapter says neither where the page icons are declared nor which files are the frame, the check logo-use reads nothing and passes, and does not say that it read nothing.

When an icon set records no sizes, status and audit name a person's step, writing the sizes into the row by hand: no command writes them, since they are a person's answer (spec 0017, question 12).

The manifest of a mark package keeps the root numbers of the mark's construction, and spec 0017 says building again from them gives the hashes listed; logo-source compares each file with the hash the manifest lists and never builds anything, so whether the numbers give the files back is for the plug to hold.

The palette a mark package's manifest lists is not compared with the root colour the repository chose, and no question is asked when they differ (spec 0017, the plug that builds a mark, point 6): a person brings it in with bring-in.

When the owner picks a mark other than the first candidate of the question on logo:<id>, the decision sheet writes the answer as a value naming that candidate, and the wall owner-calls reads only a kept answer: it says the owner answered otherwise and stays red, and logo-source names no one as having chosen, though the owner chose. Until the wall reads a value that names a candidate, the owner keeps the recommendation, or the question is asked again with the chosen mark first.
limits.closed_by: decide --ask --candidate offers the marks of logo:<id>, the recommended one first; keeping chooses the first and naming another chooses that one, and the wall reads either as the owner's choice when the branch's logo row is that candidate's (made.candidate, written by logo-source --package from the manifest's candidate) or names none and the first was kept; a refusal, words that name no offered candidate and a row of another candidate stay red, saying which; the gate, status, the decision sheet and logo-source --package name the candidate, who chose it and when (plugin 0.75.0, d0128), held by plugin tests that also compare every other item and question with the tool and scripts of 0.74.0, and on a repository whose installed tool is 0.74.0 decide refuses --candidate and names upgrade first

limits.note: The plug logo-design is declared at the brand assets socket and measured only in part, so it carries no measured entry: plugs lists it and never asks the owner to choose it (spec 0017, criterion 16). On 2026-11-27 (d0131) its remade skill ran the standard brief on two throwaway copies, one with a pinned icon set and one with nothing: it read the repository's answers, offered three marks different in structure, queued the choice as logo:<id> with candidates and stopped, and after the owner chose it left a package that its own verify and logo-source --package --dry-run accepted, every hash matching and the chooser read from the decision sheet, while the letters of its wordmark were drawn with holes that no check saw (logo-package-drawing-unchecked). No command looks at the drawing of a mark package: the plug's verify and logo-source --package compare hashes and the manifest's shape only. In the first measured run the letters of the wordmark were drawn with holes where their outlines overlap, filled by the even-odd rule, in every file that holds the text, and every check passed; an independent look at the images found it.

The mark plug outlines its wordmark only in a typeface installed on the machine, and matches it by the name the repository's font row gives. A repository that loads its heading typeface as a web font package names it as that package does (Geist Variable), while the same family installed on the machine is listed under another name (Geist): the plug reports the typeface missing even after it is installed, and the owner has to answer the name once more. Nothing ties the family the wordmark was drawn in to the font row, so a wordmark drawn in another family passes every check.

The mark plug sets the wordmark to the product's name as written and never asks in which language or script the text of a logo is to be. When the owner wants it in English or without diacritics, he says so after the package is built, and the package is built again. The plug also takes the wordmark's text and the product's name as two inputs while its page says they are one: with a wordmark of other words, the manifest's title, the brand sheet and the preview keep the name, and logo-source --package titles the row from the manifest, so the row is named by words the logo does not show.

After the owner chose a mark, the plug may draw a simpler mark for small sizes and build the page icon from it, as its own rule says when a detail is lost at 16 px. The page icon is then a drawing the owner never saw, recorded with the role mark; neither the plugin nor the plug asks him to look at it.

A mark the owner chose, whose package is built and verified but whose row is not written, is not seen by status or audit: they name the choice on the decision sheet and nothing waits for the mark. The question of who holds the right to use it appears only once logo-source --package writes the row.

The row of a mark is held only once a person writes who holds the right to use it and where. In the first measured run the owner was asked for that sentence several times, chose and answered everything else, and did not write it; the run stopped at the dry run. How the sentence is best asked for is not known.

The mark package and the files the plug writes beside it lie in the repository, and the repository's formatter check refuses some of them (the manifest, the brand sheet, its README). Formatting them breaks the hashes the package lists, so a builder adds them to the formatter's ignore file by hand; no page says so and no check reads it.

The command decide --ask on an owner's item (logo:<id>) says the gate is red until the owner answers, but the wall owner-calls holds a branch only: on the main branch, or a repository with no other branch, the gate stays green with the question open.
When the only answer that waits is the licence of a row a command wrote, status names /design-assembly:new as the next step, while the row says the licence is written by hand into the row's file.

A plug file says in a sentence what must be on the machine for the plug to run (needs machine, and the key machine), and the board shows it; no command checks that the runner or the library is there, so a plug the session holds that lacks them fails only when it runs.

Whether a pinned icon set that is a package has an icon is read from the names of the files the installed package holds: a package that keeps every icon in one file, or names its files otherwise than its icons, reads as lacking the icon, and icon-source --draw records a drawn icon the set may have.
